chapter.chapter_subtitle: Meaning, Processes, Stages, Factors, Theories of Forgetting, and Improving Memory
chapter.chapter_introduction: Welcome to Chapter 4 of General Psychology. Learning and memory are closely related — learning refers to the initial acquisition or encoding of information, while memory refers to later storage and retrieval of information. Information is learned so that it can be retrieved later, and retrieval cannot occur unless information was learned. This chapter explores memory, its processes (encoding, storage, retrieval), its stages (sensory memory, short-term memory, long-term memory), factors affecting memory, forgetting and its theories, and techniques for improving memory.

sections.section_introduction: Memory is the retention of information or what is learned earlier over time. It is the way in which we record the past for later use in the present. Let us explore the meaning, processes, and stages of memory.

subsections.subtitle: 4.1.1. Meaning and Processes of Memory
paragraphs: **Memory** is the retention of information or what is learned earlier over time. It is the way in which we record the past for later use in the present.
Memory is a blanket label for a large number of processes that form the bridges between our past and our present.
**Three basic processes of memory:**
**a) Encoding:** The process by which information is initially recorded in a form usable to memory. We transform a sensory input into a form or a memory code that can be further processed.
**b) Storage:** To be remembered, the encoded experience must leave some record in the nervous system (the memory trace). It is the location in memory system in which material is saved.

**c) Retrieval:** The point at which one tries to remember to dredge up a particular memory trace from among all the others we have stored. Material in memory storage is located, brought into awareness, and used.
**Failure to remember** can result from problems during any of the three phases of the memory process.

The process by which information is initially recorded in a form usable to memory.
The location in memory system in which material is saved.

Three processes: encoding, storage, retrieval.

Retrieval: bringing information into awareness.

subsections.subtitle: 4.1.2. Stages/Structure of Memory
paragraphs: Memory structure is the nature of memory storage itself — how information is represented in memory, how long it lasts, and how it is organized.

**1. Sensory Memory/Sensory Register:** The entryway to memory. It is the first information storage area. It acts as a holding bin, retaining information until we can select items for attention. Visual images (Iconic memory) remain for a maximum of one second. Auditory images (Echoic memory) remain for up to two seconds.

**2. Short-Term Memory (STM):** Part of our memory that holds the contents of our attention. It is active, rapidly accessible, preserves temporal sequence, and has limited capacity (7 ± 2 chunks). Information remains for up to about 30 seconds. Chunking expands working memory by grouping information into larger units.

**3. Long-Term Memory (LTM):** Memory system used for the relatively permanent storage of meaningful information. Capacity seems to have no practical limits. LTM stores information for indefinite periods — days, months, years, or a lifetime.
**Subsystems of LTM:**
- **Declarative (explicit) memory:** Conscious recollection of information (facts or events). Subdivided into semantic and episodic memories.
- **Semantic memory:** Factual knowledge (meaning of words, concepts, math).
- **Episodic memory:** Memories for events and situations from personal experience.
- **Non-declarative (implicit) memory:** Behavior affected by prior experience without conscious recollection. Includes procedural memory (knowing how to comb hair, use a pencil, or swim).
**Serial Position Effect:** Recall is best for items at the beginning (primacy effect) and at the end (recency effect) of a list. The result is a U-shaped curve.

**Explanation:** First few items are remembered because STM was relatively empty when they entered, so they were thoroughly processed. Last few items are remembered because they are still sitting in STM at the time of recall. Middle items drop out of STM before they can be stored in LTM.

subsections.subtitle: 4.1.3. Factors Affecting Memory
paragraphs: **Eleven factors that influence memory process:**
a. **Ability to retain:** Depends upon good memory traces left in the brain by past experiences.
b. **Good health:** A person with good health can retain learned material better.
c. **Age of the learner:** Youngsters can remember better than the aged.
d. **Maturity:** Very young children cannot retain and remember complex material.
e. **Will to remember:** Willingness to remember helps for better retention.
f. **Intelligence:** More intelligent person will have better memory.
g. **Interest:** If a person has more interest, he will learn and retain better.
h. **Over learning:** Experiments have proved that over learning will lead to better memory.
i. **Speed of learning:** Quicker learning leads to better retention.
j. **Meaningfulness of the material:** Meaningful materials remain in our memory for longer period than nonsense material.
k. **Sleep or rest:** Sleep or rest immediately after learning strengthens connections in the brain and helps for clear memory.

Studying information even after you think you already know it.

sections.section_introduction: Forgetting is the apparent loss of information already encoded and stored in long-term memory. In this section, we explore the meaning, concepts, and theories of forgetting.

subsections.subtitle: 4.2.1. Meaning and Concepts of Forgetting
paragraphs: **Forgetting** refers to the apparent loss of information already encoded and stored in the long-term memory.

The first attempts to study forgetting were made by German psychologist **Hermann Ebbinghaus** (1885/1913). Using himself as his only subject, he memorized lists of three-letter non-sense syllables (meaningless sets of two consonants with a vowel in between, such as FIW and BOZ).
**Ebbinghaus's findings:**
- Most rapid forgetting occurs in the first hours, and particularly in the first hour.
- After nine hours, the rate of forgetting slows and declines little, even after the passage of many days.
- Relearning of previously mastered material is almost always faster than starting from scratch.
definitions: The apparent loss of information already encoded and stored in long-term memory.
Meaningless sets of two consonants with a vowel in between.
Forgetting because we are motivated to forget something.
key_points: Forgetting: loss of information from LTM.
Ebbinghaus: first to study forgetting systematically.
Most rapid forgetting in the first hour.
Rate of forgetting slows after nine hours.
Relearning is faster than initial learning.

subsections.subtitle: 4.2.2. Theories of Forgetting
paragraphs: **1. Decay Theory:** Memory traces or engrams fade with time if they are not accessed. Decay occurs in sensory memory and short-term memory. The mere passage of time does not account well for forgetting in long-term memory.
**2. Interference Theory:** Forgetting occurs because similar items of information interfere with one another in either storage or retrieval.
- **Proactive Interference:** Information learned earlier interferes with recall of newer material.
- **Retroactive Interference:** New information interferes with the ability to remember old information.
**3. New Memory for Old/Displacement Theory:** New information entering memory can wipe out old information. Mostly associated with STM.

**4. Motivated Forgetting:** People forget because they block from consciousness those memories that are too threatening or painful to live with. Freud called this self-protective process **Repression**.

**5. Cue-Dependent Forgetting:** When we lack retrieval cues, we may feel as if we have lost the call number for an entry in the mind's library. Cues present during the initial stage of learning help us to recall the content.
definitions: Memory traces fade with time if not accessed.
Similar items of information interfere with one another.
Old information interferes with new information.
New information interferes with old information.
New information wipes out old information.
Blocking threatening or painful memories from consciousness.
Lack of retrieval cues leads to forgetting.
key_points: Five theories of forgetting: decay, interference, displacement, motivated, cue-dependent.
Decay: memory traces fade with time.
Interference: proactive (old interferes with new) and retroactive (new interferes with old).
Displacement: new information wipes out old.
Motivated forgetting: repression of threatening memories.
Cue-dependent: lack of retrieval cues.

subsections.subtitle: 4.2.3. Improving Memory
paragraphs: **Strategies for improving memory:**
1. **Pay Attention:** Often we fail to remember because we never encoded the information in the first place.
2. **Encode information in more than one way:** The more elaborate the encoding, the more memorable it will be.
3. **Add meaning:** The more meaningful the material, the more likely it is to link up with information already in LTM.
4. **Take your time:** Minimize interference by using study breaks for rest or recreation.
5. **Over learn:** Studying information even after you think you already know it is one of the best ways to ensure you will remember it.
6. **Monitor your learning:** Test yourself frequently, rehearse thoroughly, and review periodically.

Studying information even after you think you already know it.
Testing yourself frequently to assess progress.
key_points: Pay attention, encode in multiple ways, add meaning.

exercises.question: Define memory and forgetting.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Memory: retention of information over time. Forgetting: apparent loss of information from LTM.
• Explanation & Derivation:
  - Memory processes: encoding, storage, retrieval.
  - Forgetting: loss of information already encoded and stored.
• Final Answer: Memory is the retention of information over time. Forgetting is the loss of information from long-term memory.

exercises.question: Describe the stage memory model proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Three stages: sensory memory, short-term memory, long-term memory.
• Explanation & Derivation:
  - Sensory memory: iconic (1 sec), echoic (2 sec).
  - STM: 7 ± 2 chunks, 30 seconds.
  - LTM: unlimited capacity, indefinite duration.
• Final Answer: The stage model includes sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory.

exercises.question: Explain the typical characteristics of sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Characteristics of each memory stage.
• Explanation & Derivation:
  - Sensory memory: brief (1-2 sec), large capacity, unprocessed.
  - STM: active, rapid access, limited capacity (7 ± 2), 30 seconds.
  - LTM: permanent, unlimited capacity, meaningful information.
• Final Answer: Sensory memory is brief and unprocessed; STM is limited and active; LTM is permanent and unlimited.

exercises.question: Discuss how learned information are organized in the long-term memory store.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: LTM subsystems: declarative and non-declarative.
• Explanation & Derivation:
  - Declarative (explicit): semantic (facts) and episodic (events).
  - Non-declarative (implicit): procedural (skills).
• Final Answer: LTM is organized into declarative (semantic and episodic) and non-declarative (procedural) memory.

exercises.question: List down the theories of forgetting and elaborate the main ideas of each theory.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Five theories of forgetting.
• Explanation & Derivation:
  - Decay: memory traces fade with time.
  - Interference: proactive and retroactive interference.
  - Displacement: new information wipes out old.
  - Motivated forgetting: repression of threatening memories.
  - Cue-dependent: lack of retrieval cues.
• Final Answer: The theories are decay, interference, displacement, motivated forgetting, and cue-dependent forgetting.
